# QP-04 Bean receiving and release procedure Date: 5 January 2026 Prepared by: Marcus Bell For: Quality and warehouse staff ## 1. Purpose Every lot of cocoa beans must be checked and released by Quality before Production may use it. This procedure sets the checks, limits and decisions. ## 2. Receiving steps 1\. Weigh and inspect. Logistics weighs every bag and notes damage, wet or stained jute, odors and pests on the receiving note. 2\. Sample. Quality draws a composite sample from every bag (0.5-1 kg in total, booked as a deduction from the lot). 3\. Moisture. Measure with the calibrated moisture meter (% wet basis). 4\. Cut test. Cut 300 beans lengthwise and classify each one: well fermented, partly fermented, slaty, purple, mouldy, insect-damaged, germinated or flat. 5\. Sensory check. Bench-roast and taste with at least three tasters. 6\. Decide: release, hold or reject (section 4). ## 3. Limits
CHECK LIMIT
Moisture 7.5% maximum
Mouldy beans 3% maximum (9 of 300)
Slaty beans 5% maximum (15 of 300)
Insect-damaged beans 3% maximum (9 of 300)
Off-flavors Any smoky, hammy or musty off-flavor confirmed by at least three tasters rejects the lot

## 4. Decisions

. Release: all checks pass. Quality signs the lot release record; only then can Production issue the beans.

. Hold: the lot is over the moisture limit but otherwise acceptable. Mark the bags HOLD, move them to the
bean conditioning room and re-dry in shallow trays with dehumidification. Retest moisture (and send a
sample to an independent lab for moisture and microbiology). Release when moisture is at or below 7.5%.

. Reject: cut-test limits exceeded or an off-flavor confirmed. Raise a nonconformance report, notify
Sourcing, and apply the supplier contract (sample-match clause). Rejected beans are never blended into
other lots.


## 5. Records

Receiving note (Logistics), receiving register, hold notice, conditioning-room log, lab certificate, lot release
record, nonconformance report.

# SPEC-01 Cocoa bean quality specification for suppliers Date: 5 January 2026 Prepared by: Marcus Bell For: Suppliers This specification is part of every Cocoarynth supply contract. ## 1. Product Dried, fermented cocoa beans (Theobroma cacao) of the agreed origin, packed in new, clean jute bags of about 60 kg, each marked with the lot code. ## 2. Quality limits
PARAMETER LIMIT
Moisture 7.5% maximum on arrival
Well fermented (cut test, 300 beans) 75% minimum target
Mouldy 3% maximum
Slaty 5% maximum
Insect-damaged 3% maximum
Foreign matter 1% maximum
Off-flavors None (smoky, hammy, musty, chemical)
Microbiology Salmonella not detected in 25 g; yeast and mould ≤ 1 x 104 CFU/g
## 3. Sample match Before each new supplier or new season, the supplier sends a 2 kg pre-shipment sample. If a shipped lot does not match the approved sample in flavor, Cocoarynth may reject it with full credit to Cocoarynth. The supplier is responsible for disposal or return costs. ## 4. Good drying practice . Dry beans on raised beds, mats or patios - never directly on the ground. . Keep drying beans away from smoke, exhaust, fuel and chemicals. Wood or fuel-fired dryers must vent their smoke well away from and above the drying area. . Cover beans during rain and do not bag them until they are fully dry. ## 5. Records The supplier keeps collection tickets, fermentation and drying records for each lot and shares them on request. Owner: Marcus Bell, Quality Manager.

# Origin profile: Río Claro, Esmeraldas, Ecuador Date: 1 April 2026 Prepared by: Ana Ortega For: Cocoarynth staff and retail partners Cocoarynth has bought cacao from Esmeraldas, on Ecuador's northern Pacific coast, since 2018. Our partner there is the Cooperativa Agroartesanal Río Claro, a cooperative of 86 smallholder families that collects freshly harvested beans from its members, ferments and dries them at a central collection center, and exports them to us through Guayaquil. # Sensory panel report: 2026 single-origin bars

Date: 24 September 2026

Prepared by: Devi Narayan

For: Company-wide


## Method

Our annual panel tasted every single-origin bar on 22 September 2026. Nine trained panelists from Quality,
Production and Sales tasted 5 g pieces of each 70 g bar at 20 °C in individual booths. Samples carried
random three-digit codes, so no one knew which origin they were tasting. Each panelist scored seven flavor
attributes from 0 (absent) to 10 (very strong), checked for off-flavors, and gave an overall quality score from 0
to 10.

## Discussion

Madagascar Tsaravola 70% was the clear winner, with an overall score of 8.4. Seven of nine panelists
ranked it first. Panelists described red berry and raspberry, citrus zest, bright but balanced acidity and low
bitterness. It had the highest fruit score of any bar (8.5) and one of the lowest bitterness scores (3.0).

Ecuador Río Claro 72% came second (7.9) with the strongest floral character. Ghana Akwapim Ridge 68%
scored lower overall (7.2) but was voted the most "chocolatey" bar, with the highest cocoa (8.0) and nutty
(6.0) scores.

# Cocoarynth sourcing principles

Date: 1 September 2025

Prepared by: Ana Ortega

For: Public and staff


## What we believe

Our bars have two ingredients, so flavor starts on the farm. We buy beans for their flavor and the care that
goes into them, and we pay for that care.


## Our principles

1\. Pay for quality, not volume. We pay well above the world commodity price, and we add bonuses when
fermentation and drying are excellent.

2\. Know the farms. We buy from cooperatives, associations and estates that can tell us which farms
contributed to each lot.

3\. Stay for the long term. We aim to buy from each partner year after year, so they can plan and invest.

4\. Invest together. Premiums fund practical improvements: drying frames, greenhouse dryers, hedges and
training.

5\. Be honest about claims. We only make certification claims we can prove on the day a bar is packed.

6\. Be transparent. We publish our average landed prices against the world reference every year.


## How we judge whether a premium is worth it

A higher price for beans is justified when:

. the beans give a distinctive, high-scoring flavor at our blind sensory panel; and

. customers and retailers are willing to pay more for the bar, so the premium is sustainable for us as well as
the grower.

If an origin costs more but does not stand out in tasting or sales, we work with the supplier on quality before
we reconsider the relationship.

Owner: Ana Ortega, Head of Sourcing.

# Chocolate storage and handling guide Date: 1 October 2025 Prepared by: Marcus Bell For: Staff, carriers and retailers ## Keep it cool, dry and steady
CONDITION TARGET
Temperature 15-20 °C in storage, in transit and on display
Relative humidity Below 60%
Light Out of direct sunlight
Odors Away from produce, coffee, cleaning products and fuel
Changes Avoid quick moves from cold to warm

## What is bloom?

Bloom is a whitish, grey or streaky film on the surface of chocolate. It is safe to eat, but bloomed bars look
old and cannot be sold as first-quality product.


Fat bloom: grey, dusty, streaky surface.

![](figures/1.2 "- Rectangular dark chocolate bar on brown paper. - Surface appearance: grey, dusty, streaky coating visible across the top. - Background: metal table with perforated pattern; blurred shelves and boxes.")


<!-- PageFooter: Cocoarynth Chocolate Works . Chocolate storage and handling guide -->
<!-- PageNumber: Page 1 of 3 -->
<!-- PageBreak -->


Well-tempered chocolate in good condition: glossy and even.

![](figures/2.1 "Chocolate bar partially wrapped in brown paper on a light-colored surface. Bar: dark brown, rectangular, segmented into 8 visible squares arranged 2 by 4. Surface appearance: glossy and even. Wrapper: folded brown paper beneath and over the top portion of the bar. No visible labels, numeric scales, units, axes, or category names.")


Fat bloom (heat bloom). When chocolate gets warm, some of the cocoa butter melts and moves to the
surface, where it re-crystallizes as dull grey streaks and blotches. The risk rises sharply above 25 °C, even if
the bars never look melted. A few hours in a hot truck, depot or shop window is enough.

Sugar bloom. When cold chocolate is moved into warm, humid air, moisture condenses on the surface,
dissolves a little sugar and leaves a dry, white, dusty film when it evaporates. Avoid by letting cartons warm
up slowly before opening.


Sugar bloom: dry, powdery white dusting with spots where condensation dried. Unlike fat bloom, it feels gritty, not greasy.

![](figures/2.2 "Rectangular dark chocolate bar partially inside a brown paper wrapper. Top surface shows a dry, powdery white dusting with multiple irregular round white spots. Bar is angled diagonally from upper left to lower right. Background is light gray. No visible labels, numeric scales, units, axes, or category names.")


## Rules for carriers

1\. Ship in refrigerated or insulated vehicles set to 15-20 °C.

2\. Never stage chocolate in unrefrigerated areas such as overflow bays, docks or yards, even for "a few
hours".

3\. If a cold room is full, call Cocoarynth Logistics before moving the pallet.

4\. Keep the temperature logger on the pallet and return it with the delivery paperwork.

# POL-03 Label and marketing claims policy Date: 15 January 2026 Prepared by: Marcus Bell For: All staff ## 1. Origin claims 3.1 Single origin. A bar may be called single-origin only if all of its cocoa comes from one country and one growing region, bought from one supplier. Our four current origins cover floral (Ecuador), classic cocoa (Ghana), citrus and honey (Peru) and red fruit

we are trialing beans from the Dominican Republic to fill that gap.

The Asociación de Productores de Cacao Loma Verde groups 38 farmers in Hato Mayor province. Unlike our

Batch One production run of one bar. Its code is printed on the wrapper as the lot code, e.g. EC26-0811 (origin, year, month and day).

Bloom A grey or white film on chocolate. Fat bloom comes from warmth; sugar bloom from condensation. Safe to eat, but not first quality.
Collection ticket (boleta de acopio) The paper slip written when a farmer delivers fresh beans to a cooperative. Shows farm, weight and lot.
Cut test Cutting 300 beans in half to check fermentation and defects.
Hold A bean lot that cannot be used until Quality resolves a problem, such as high moisture.
Landed cost What we pay per kg of beans delivered to our factory, including freight and import.
Mouldy bean A bean with visible mould inside when cut.
Release Quality's sign-off that a bean lot or batch may be used or sold.
Sample match Contract clause letting us reject a lot that does not taste like the approved sample.
Sell-in Bars we sell to retailers (not what retailers sell to shoppers).
Single origin All cocoa from one region and supplier - usually several farms.
Slaty bean A grey, unfermented bean when cut; tastes bitter and astringent.
Transaction certificate A certifier's document proving a specific shipment is organic.
Wrapper lot code The batch code printed on the back of every bar.
